summary.text: Take \(n=0\): \(\Phi_1(0)=-1\), while \(\Phi_k(0)=1\) for every \(k>1\), so in every positive-index case the absolute value is \(1\), which is not prime.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(n,k)=\left|\Phi_k(n)\right|,
\]
where \(\Phi_k(X)\) is the \(k\)-th cyclotomic polynomial over \(\mathbb Z\), and absolute value is taken because the formal assertion tests the natural absolute value of the integer evaluation. The proposition actually formalized is
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N\;\exists k\in\mathbb N,
\qquad k>0\quad\text{and}\quad P(n,k)\text{ is prime}.
\tag{1}
\]
Here \(\mathbb N\) contains \(0\). We disprove (1) by taking \(n=0\).

We first determine every cyclotomic polynomial at zero. For any polynomial
\[
f(X)=c_0+c_1X+\cdots+c_rX^r,
\]
one has \(f(0)=c_0\), its constant coefficient. Thus \(\Phi_k(0)\) is just the constant coefficient of \(\Phi_k\).

For \(k=1\),
\[
\Phi_1(X)=X-1,
\]
so
\[
\Phi_1(0)=-1.
\tag{2}
\]
For every \(k>1\), the constant coefficient of \(\Phi_k\) is \(1\), and hence
\[
\Phi_k(0)=1.
\tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this constant-coefficient fact follows from the standard cyclotomic factorization
\[
X^k-1=\prod_{d\mid k}\Phi_d(X).
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, it can be proved by strong induction on \(k>1\). Evaluating (4) at \(X=0\) shows that the product of the constant coefficients of all \(\Phi_d\) with \(d\mid k\) is \(-1\). Among the proper divisors of \(k\), the divisor \(1\) contributes \(-1\) by (2), while every proper divisor \(d>1\) contributes \(1\) by the induction hypothesis. Consequently, the product of the constant coefficients belonging to all proper divisors of \(k\) is \(-1\). If \(c_k\) denotes the constant coefficient of \(\Phi_k\), equation (4) at zero therefore gives
\[
-1=c_k(-1),
\]
so \(c_k=1\), proving (3).

The polynomial convention used in the formal statement also defines the zeroth cyclotomic polynomial by
\[
\Phi_0(X)=1,
\]
so \(\Phi_0(0)=1\). This case is not needed for a prospective witness, because (1) requires \(k>0\), but it shows that the same absolute-value conclusion holds for every natural-number index. Combining all three possible cases gives
\[
\left|\Phi_k(0)\right|=
\begin{cases}
|1|=1,&k=0,\\
|-1|=1,&k=1,\\
|1|=1,&k>1.
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]
In particular, for every positive integer \(k\),
\[
P(0,k)=\left|\Phi_k(0)\right|=1.
\]
But \(1\) is not prime: by definition a prime natural number must be greater than \(1\) (equivalently, \(1\) is a unit and has no status as a prime). Therefore there is no positive \(k\) for which \(P(0,k)\) is prime.

Now suppose (1) were true. Applying it to \(n=0\) would provide a positive \(k\) such that \(\left|\Phi_k(0)\right|\) is prime. Equation (5) says that this number is \(1\), contradicting the fact that \(1\) is not prime. Hence
\[
\neg\left(\forall n\in\mathbb N\;\exists k>0,
\ \left|\Phi_k(n)\right|\text{ is prime}\right).
\]
Thus the universally quantified formal assertion is false, with \(n=0\) as a counterexample.

There is an important scope distinction. The canonical OEIS conjecture asks about every positive integer \(n\), whereas the formal assertion above quantifies over all natural numbers and therefore includes \(n=0\). The counterexample \(n=0\) disproves the formal assertion exactly as written, but it is not a counterexample to the positive-\(n\) conjecture. If the intended domain is \(n\ge 1\), this argument leaves that intended conjecture unresolved.
